judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 68. It limits arguments valuing pain-and-suffering damages, requires dismissal rulings within 90 days, allows voluntary dismissal only before day 60 after an answer, and prevents double recovery of legal fees. It allows seat-belt evidence, requires strong proof of similar past conduct for unsafe-property claims, limits medical awards to necessary care's fair value, and allows some trials to split issues into stages. The Georgia House passed it 91-82, and it became law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against Senate Bill 68. It allows seat-belt evidence, requires strong proof of similar past conduct for unsafe-property claims, limits medical awards to necessary care's fair value, and allows some trials to split issues into stages. The Georgia House passed it 91-82, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes to accept the House's version of Senate Bill 68, Georgia's lawsuit overhaul. The Senate agreed 34-21, the last step before the governor, and it became law as Act 9. Lawyers may no longer argue a dollar figure for pain and suffering. A judge must decide a motion to dismiss within 90 days after written arguments end. A plaintiff may drop a case alone only before the 60th day after the other side answers. Juries may now hear whether an injured person wore a seat belt. Property owners face a tougher test before they can be blamed for a crime on their land. Payment for medical care is limited to the reasonable value of the care actually needed. Some trials may be split, with fault decided before damages.
judgments.nay_description: Voted no on accepting the House's version of Senate Bill 68, Georgia's lawsuit overhaul. The Senate agreed 34-21 anyway, and it became law as Act 9. Property owners face a tougher test before they can be blamed for a crime on their land. Payment for medical care is limited to the reasonable value of the care actually needed. Some trials may be split, with fault decided before damages.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1. The Riley Gaines Act of 2025 makes Georgia schools and colleges label each sports team male, female, or coed, and bars males from female teams and, with exceptions, females from male college teams. At competitions, restrooms, changing areas, and overnight sleeping quarters must be set aside by sex, with reasonable alternatives offered. Colleges may not give males scholarships meant for female players, and state law replaces the word gender with sex. The Georgia House passed it 100-64, and it became law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against Senate Bill 1. The Riley Gaines Act of 2025 makes Georgia schools and colleges label each sports team male, female, or coed, and bars males from female teams and, with exceptions, females from male college teams. At competitions, restrooms, changing areas, and overnight sleeping quarters must be set aside by sex, with reasonable alternatives offered. Colleges may not give males scholarships meant for female players, and state law replaces the word gender with sex. The Georgia House passed it 100-64, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes to accept the House's version of Senate Bill 1, the Riley Gaines Act of 2025. The Georgia Senate agreed 34-20 and it became law as Act 11. Schools, school systems, private schools that compete with them, and colleges must label each team male, female, or coed. Males may not play on a team labeled female. At school competitions, shared restrooms, changing areas, and sleeping quarters must be set aside by sex. Schools must offer another option to a student unwilling or unable to use the space for their sex. The law defines sex as biological sex. It does not let schools check a student's body to confirm sex, though medical records may be used.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 185. It bars state money or resources from paying for prisoners' sex-change surgery, hormone therapy, or products that change sex traits. Exceptions cover unrelated needed care, certain sex-development conditions, and a gradual stop for prisoners already on hormones when the law begins. The Georgia Senate passed it 37-15, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 144. A pesticide maker generally satisfies its health-warning duty by using a label approved by the United States Environmental Protection Agency or matching the federal health-risk review. That protection ends if the agency finds the maker knowingly hid, misstated, concealed, or destroyed important health-risk information to get or keep approval. The Georgia Senate passed it 42-12, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 212. Georgia schools cannot give student directory information to candidates, campaign committees, political action committees, or political groups. Disclosing confidential voter registration information to an unauthorized person becomes a felony punishable by one to ten years, a fine up to $100,000, or both. Candidates and committees also cannot ask minors to fraudulently organize campaign events on school property. The Senate version made anyone who told students about voter or Selective Service military-draft registration, or helped them register, attest in writing that they act for no political group and will share no student data. The House later narrowed that duty to people who both tell and help, and exempted people attending public events. The Georgia Senate passed it 33-19, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's final version of HB 1247, the 'Georgia Bureaucratic Deference Elimination Act.' The Georgia House agreed 98-70 and the bill became law as Act 718. The law bars courts from deferring to a state agency's own reading of laws and rules. Its 'Red Tape Rollback Act of 2026' sets new steps for writing rules. It also makes each agency send the Office of Planning and Budget a review of its own rules. The law opens to the public any settlement of an unlawful employment practice claim against a member of the General Assembly. The claimant's name is removed, but the member is named. A separate part requires some privately funded groups that shelter or serve homeless people to take part in Georgia's Homeless Management Information System. That duty is narrow. It reaches only groups within 1,000 feet of a school, college, child care center, public park, or playground. It applies in one metro area, not statewide, and skips groups that served fewer than ten people in the past year. A group that does not take part gets a non-criminal citation.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 443. Purposely or recklessly blocking a highway or street so it cannot be passed, then refusing a peace officer's or other official's request to clear it, becomes a high and aggravated misdemeanor. The same conduct on a sidewalk or other public passage stays a plain misdemeanor. A violator may also be held liable in a civil suit for damages caused by the offense. The Georgia Senate passed it 35-17, and it became law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against Senate Bill 443. Purposely or recklessly blocking a highway or street so it cannot be passed, then refusing a peace officer's or other official's request to clear it, becomes a high and aggravated misdemeanor. The same conduct on a sidewalk or other public passage stays a plain misdemeanor. A violator may also be held liable in a civil suit for damages caused by the offense. The Georgia Senate passed it 35-17, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 443. It made purposely or recklessly blocking a highway or street a high and aggravated misdemeanor, a more serious grade of minor crime. Blocking a sidewalk or other public passage stayed a plain misdemeanor. The crime applies only when a person refuses to clear the way after an officer's order. A violator may also be sued for damages caused by the blockage. The Georgia House passed it 96-69, completing passage. It became law as Act 512, effective July 1, 2026.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against passing Senate Bill 443. The bill raised blocking a highway or street to a high and aggravated misdemeanor, a more serious grade of minor crime. Blocking a sidewalk or other public passage stayed a plain misdemeanor. The offense applies only when a person refuses to clear the way after an officer's order. It also let people harmed sue the blocker for damages. The Georgia House passed it 96-69 anyway, and it became law as Act 512.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 552, the True Patriotism and Universal Student Access (TPUSA) Act. It lets public school students form political clubs and hold political meetings on the same terms as other clubs unrelated to classes. A school that allows such clubs must give them the same use of rooms and the same chance to announce meetings. Schools may not treat a student group worse because of the political content of its speech. Students may wear political messages if the dress code allows other messages. Schools keep their power to maintain order, discipline, and attendance. The Georgia House passed this House version 95-68, the Senate agreed the same day, and it became law as Act 497.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against passing Senate Bill 552, the True Patriotism and Universal Student Access (TPUSA) Act. The law lets public school students organize political clubs and meetings on the same terms as other non-class clubs. Schools that allow those clubs must give them equal use of rooms and equal chances to announce meetings. Schools may not discriminate based on the political content of student speech. Political clothing gets the same treatment as other messages under the dress code. The Georgia House passed it 95-68 and it became law as Act 497, effective July 1, 2026.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes to pass Senate Bill 472, a school money-oversight bill. The Georgia House passed it 96-58 and it became law as Act 722. The law lets the State Board of Education ask the governor to suspend local school board members, with pay. That follows state auditor findings of money mismanagement or the worst level of state monitoring. In districts flagged as high risk, a superintendent's contract may not run longer than 12 months. Some auditor findings became grounds to fire a superintendent for cause. Early advances of state money are capped at half the district's state funds from the year before. State auditors must audit every local school system and state charter school each year.
judgments.nay_description: Voted no on Senate Bill 472, a school money-oversight bill. The Georgia House passed it 96-58 anyway and it became law as Act 722. The law lets the State Board of Education ask the governor to suspend local school board members, with pay. State auditors must audit every local school system and state charter school each year.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes, 29-17, when the Georgia Senate accepted the House rewrite of Senate Bill 472. The law lets the State Board of Education ask the governor to suspend local school board members, with pay. That follows state auditors putting a district under the highest level of monitoring, or finding financial mismanagement or misconduct. In districts labeled high risk, a superintendent's contract may be extended only 12 months at a time. Certain auditor findings become grounds for firing a superintendent for cause. The state may advance a district no more than half its prior year's funding outside the normal schedule. Every local school system and state charter school must get a yearly financial and compliance audit. The House rewrite also cut the voter petition needed to force an election on dissolving a city school system from one-fourth of voters to 10 percent. It became law as Act 722.
judgments.nay_description: Voted no, 29-17, when the Georgia Senate accepted the House rewrite of Senate Bill 472. The Senate accepted it anyway. The law lets the State Board of Education ask the governor to suspend local school board members, with pay. That follows state auditors putting a district under the highest level of monitoring, or finding financial mismanagement or misconduct. In districts labeled high risk, a superintendent's contract may be extended only 12 months at a time. Certain auditor findings become grounds for firing a superintendent for cause. The state may advance a district no more than half its prior year's funding outside the normal schedule. Every local school system and state charter school must get a yearly financial and compliance audit. The House rewrite also cut the voter petition needed to force an election on dissolving a city school system from one-fourth of voters to 10 percent. It became law as Act 722.
